title: Leaving Traces
subtitle: Transforming Past Wounds into Future Strength
summary: Leaving Traces proposes collective ecological restoration as a form of remembrance. At ChesLen Preserve, historical storytelling and the shared care of living landscapes connect the Underground Railroad’s legacy of mutual aid with future generations.
story: In Chester County, the history of the Underground Railroad runs through a landscape of fields, wooded slopes, and creek valleys. For people escaping slavery, these environments could offer concealment, expose movement, or influence where and when they could travel. Their journeys depended on a close reading of the land and networks of mutual aid. Today, this history meets a changing landscape, where erosion, flooding, and habitat degradation call for renewed collective care.

Leaving Traces proposes ecological restoration as a living practice of remembrance. With ChesLen Preserve as a pilot for the Brandywine Greenway, the project brings residents, students, historians, and land stewards together to care for the places through which these histories are understood. Together, they would restore serpentine grasslands, create stormwater basins that support birds, and build woody structures that slow runoff, capture sediment, and improve firefly habitat. Shared labor becomes a way to carry the legacy of mutual aid into the present landscape.

Memory is encountered through the body: in the movement between open fields and wooded slopes, the sound of an owl beyond the trees, or the changing visibility of a woodland at dusk. Guided walks bring these encounters into conversation with documented accounts of movement, concealment, and survival. Seasonal change gives each return a different character, allowing historical interpretation and ecological observation to unfold together.

Over time, the work leaves traces of its own. A tended grassland, a planted slope, or a pool that holds water records acts of care that others will inherit. Seasonal stewardship and commemorative gatherings invite each generation to return, learn, and contribute. Remembrance takes shape through this repeated exchange between people and place, carrying the Underground Railroad’s legacy of mutual aid into the care of future landscapes.

narrative.title: Storytelling Center
paragraphs: The Storytelling Center proposes a temporary place for histories to be encountered and carried onward. Walls assembled from locally salvaged timber enclose a floor inscribed with gathered historical accounts and oral memories of the Underground Railroad. Above them, a suspended wax ceiling places the room within the changing light and warmth of each day.

In the proposed material cycle, sunlight gradually warms and softens the wax. As it descends, the ceiling opens to more light while the words below become obscured. What makes the room more visible also makes its stories less legible. Returning visitors encounter an altered surface: a passage read one day may be partly covered the next, until accumulated wax buries the inscriptions.

The enclosure, too, is conceived to weather and eventually disappear within the continuing cycles of day and night. Its impermanence holds the vulnerability of memory in view. As the physical traces recede, the work of remembrance passes to those who have read, listened, and gathered here. What remains depends on the stories they carry beyond the walls, and on their willingness to tell them again.

title: Soil Holds: Matter, Memory, Commons
location: Angel’s Knoll, Los Angeles, California, United States
summary: A proposal for Angel’s Knoll connects soil repair, urban memory, and community stewardship through an accessible landscape shaped by ongoing care.
story: Bunker Hill was cut down to build a city, and what remains is soil. The soil at Angel’s Knoll has outlasted every attempt to erase, stabilize, and pave around it. Damaged and compacted, this persistent ground forms the project’s foundation, treated as living matter, relationship, and memory.

As matter, the hill operates as a dynamic, heterogeneous field, spanning flat plateaus, sharp inclines, and shifting solar exposures. Here, site clearing initiates a material metabolism: organic debris is cycled upward to nourish preserved vegetation at the crest, while descending the slope, the physical reshaping intensifies. The ground fractures into a textured patchwork of micro-conditions, secured by varied erosion controls. Native bands bind the ground between open plots left to succeed on their own, where the slow labor of becoming soil stays in view. This is provisional ground, built without knowing the outcome and left to inherit its form.

This ongoing repair also catalyzes social connection. Occupying a sharp urban threshold between the elevated corporate plateau and historic downtown, the reconstructed soil bridges contrasting realities. We treat the balance between ecological labor and public life as an evolving relationship. Initially, the hill serves as an exposed working ground, inviting the city to work and witness the labor of rebuilding. Over time, soil rebuilding softens into everyday, recreational stewardship; observation matures into active belonging as surrounding communities merge with the site’s ongoing care—bringing compost, tending trees, and gathering seeds to disperse its renewed vitality.

Operating as memory, the hill reveals a composite of deep geology and urban remains. Miocene marine sedimentary rock, fragments of old retaining walls, and Alberhill fire clay bricks are daylighted across the landscape. These displaced remnants of Bunker Hill form a mosaic where erased history resurfaces. Yet, collective memory demands equal access. The steep incline is sculpted into a choreographed terrain. By supporting climbing, descending, perching, and gathering, the design transforms an impassable barrier into an inclusive landscape—allowing all bodies to navigate, rest within, and inhabit the city’s layered ground.

title: Ground in Friction
summary: At Victoria Harbour, shifting dredge sediments, tidal habitats, and a grid of corten columns bring ecological processes into friction with the ordering systems of Melbourne’s industrial waterfront.
story: Built on the filled remains of the West Melbourne Swamp, Docklands is a landscape repeatedly remade to suppress uncertainty. What was once a saltwater lagoon, marsh, and estuarine mudflat was successively drained, dredged, indexed, and parcelled into port infrastructure and later a financialized waterfront precinct. In this process, dynamic ground was converted into something stable, legible, and tradable. Complexity was not erased so much as compressed into image: a waterfront made to appear orderly, permanent, and governable.

This proposal refuses to produce another resolved image of place. Instead, it treats landscape as a critical medium for exposing conflicting regimes of ground. Docklands is not approached as a site awaiting a new identity, but as contested land shaped by incompatible ways of understanding and using it: Country as relational and living; port territory as measurable and logistical; and contemporary waterfront urbanism as spectacle, asset, and managed lifestyle. The project does not reconcile these positions into a polite narrative, but places them in friction.

That friction begins with the ground itself. Sedimentary dredge material, historically used to overwrite wetland ecologies, is returned to the site not as stabilizing fill but as loose substrate open to settlement, erosion, and tidal variation. As it settles unevenly, targeted topographic interventions establish an ecological gradient spanning drier uplands, high and low marshes, and intertidal mudflats. Each zone supports specific faunal assemblages while preparing for climatic realities. Strategic high points are retained to provide a landward runway for marsh migration, aligned with 0.8 metres of sea-level rise by 2100. Ground is redefined as an active process of accretion and seasonal change rather than a finished surface.

Juxtaposed against this unstable field is a maritime order. A grid of corten columns, inscribed with the numerical indexing of port logistics and embedded in the paving, extends across the site as an ordering device. Reinforcing this logic, the reconstructed frame of a demolished shed registers the industrial past while attempting to impose structure on fluid terrain. The exposed seafloor functions as a palimpsest of swamp residue, maritime debris, and contemporary urban traces, revealing the layered history the site was designed to conceal. Yet these elements fail to master the landscape; as sediments shift and water levels fluctuate, the grid becomes misaligned, partially submerged, and reabsorbed as a vertical armature for emerging habitats.

As this system of control reveals its limits, the surrounding skyline—the ultimate symbol of real-estate certainty and spectacle—is subverted. The project reduces the city to background noise: through tall marsh vegetation and uneven terrain, visitors lose the continuous visual command typical of waterfronts. Openings in the foliage frame the towers and infrastructure not as triumphant vistas, but as abrupt interruptions.

Ultimately, this is neither a nostalgic restoration of the swamp nor the fabrication of a unified identity. The project reconfigures the site as contested ground, holding competing attitudes toward land in confrontation. Acting as a provocation rather than a finished destination, it poses a critical question: what kind of relationship to land should shape Docklands next?

title: The Latent Ground: Restaging Tilla-Durieux Park for Ecological Emergence
summary: Tilla-Durieux-Park becomes an unfinished ecological performance: a landscape shaped by changing soils, wind, water, and succession, opening new possibilities for public life and non-human species.
story: Tilla-Durieux-Park is reimagined not as a preserved object or a generic climate-adaptive landscape, but as an unfinished ecological performance. The original 450-metre grass sculpture, once defined by a fixed tilted plane, is transformed into an environmental instrument shaped by succession, dispersal, wind, water, maintenance, and public occupation.

At the district scale, ecological continuity is understood as a dispersal field. Seeds, pollen, insects, birds, and water move among three ecological hotspots: Potsdamer Platz, Tiergarten, and the Landwehr Canal. A future tram allows excess road space at Potsdamer Platz to be converted into planted, pedestrian, and cycling infrastructure, while Tiergarten and the canal act as contrasting reservoirs of woodland, meadow, wetland, and ruderal species. Henriette-Herz-Park and Tilla-Durieux-Park become receiving and mixing grounds where these ecologies overlap under different soil and moisture conditions.

Mobility is integrated into this framework. The tram restructures streets as civic and ecological spaces, while a new bridge connects Park am Gleisdreieck to the site through accessible human routes and quieter passages for non-human species.

At the site scale, the park’s original topography is inverted, creating lower, wetter ends and a higher, drier center. The depressions collect rainwater, receive wind and seeds, support mist and evaporative cooling, and strengthen connections to surrounding urban and canal landscapes. The central ridge contains varied sandy, rubble-rich, compacted, and woodland-edge soils that enable unpredictable plant succession rather than fixed planting beds.

Moving south, formal definition decreases as ecological openness increases. Preservation is therefore reframed as active negotiation. Through changing soils, wind-driven dispersal, disturbance, and managed succession, the park retains its sculptural and historical identity while remaining deliberately open to ecological and social change. Ruderal vegetation makes Berlin’s cycles of construction, destruction, abandonment, and control materially visible, allowing history to persist through living processes rather than static form.

title: Not Quite Order
location: Maja Park, Benjamin Franklin Parkway, Philadelphia, United States
summary: Sculptural perches, feeders, sand baths, and water basins invite birds into the Benjamin Franklin Parkway, introducing ecological diversity and new ways for people and other species to share public space.
story: For decades, the Benjamin Franklin Parkway—the city’s most monumental corridor—has projected a carefully maintained image of civic perfection. Its classical architecture, regimented rows of trees, and expansive, manicured lawns communicate a clear message: dignity through order. Within this frame, plants are treated as static design elements rather than living systems—green surfaces that stabilize a grand, controlled vision. Yet, despite its sweeping scale, the Parkway supports a strikingly narrow range of species compared to the city’s unmanaged corners. It is a space that does not merely look controlled; it subtly implies behavior, defining who—and what—is expected to belong.

To foster a more inclusive public realm, the proposal broadens the Parkway’s pristine image by introducing a layer of ecological messiness. Birds are invited as active agents whose movements and daily rituals gradually bring spontaneous diversity into the landscape, loosening its long-standing monocultural stability. Along the curving path rising from Maja Park, a series of sculptural installations reimagines familiar bird infrastructure—perches, feeders, sand baths, and water basins—as vibrant, tactile objects made of tabby concrete and painted steel.

These interventions are choreographed to foster new modes of noticing and sharing space with birds. Some elements sit low enough to encounter while sitting in the grass; others align at eye level; others draw attention upward to perching points above. These shifts in height and distance change how visitors move, pause, and look—briefly asking people to experience the Parkway from a non-human perspective. By doing so, the installation proposes a subtle reorientation of the parkway's identity. Rather than dissolving its historical grandeur, the project introduces a layer of ecological vitality that softens its rigidity. It reframes the Parkway not as a perfected image to be defended, but as a living public landscape capable of holding multiple species, multiple publics, and a more expansive idea of belonging.

title: From Ruins to Roots
location: Akademika Pavlova Station, Saltivskyi District, Kharkiv, Ukraine
summary: From Ruins to Roots reimagines vacant land around Kharkiv’s Akademika Pavlova Station as flexible public space for shelter, community connection, and long-term recovery.
story: Russia’s war in Ukraine has devastated cities and frayed social trust. Modern conflict targets minds as well as infrastructure, using misinformation to polarize communities. Meeting basic needs is urgent, yet cohesion must be rebuilt in parallel—and landscape architects are central to that work. Drawing on Operation Enduring Freedom, where park upgrades and reforestation helped stabilize daily life, this project reimagines metro stations as dual-purpose hubs for shelter and connection, fostering resilience during conflict and laying the groundwork for postwar recovery through adaptive, community-led interventions. In Kharkiv, metro stations have become lifelines during the ongoing conflict, providing 24/7 humanitarian aid. These deeply buried spaces offer safety, but prolonged confinement can heighten isolation and anxiety. Despite their protection, people still need access to outdoor public spaces. With many typical gathering places destroyed, the vacant areas surrounding metro stations offer opportunities for daylight, fresh air, and safe social interaction.

This project centers on Akademika Pavlova Station along the Saltivska Metro Line, located in Saltivskyi District—one of Kharkiv’s largest and most heavily damaged residential areas, marked by limited public space and fragmented commercial activity. The station lies near low-rise housing with insufficient access to shelter and ongoing humanitarian support. Its surroundings, dominated by expansive parking lots, present great potential for redevelopment.

These vacant lots offer opportunities for surgical interventions that can transform them into public amenities, fostering community connection and resilience during conflict. Community-driven recovery is essential for both individual healing and rebuilding social bonds. Empowering residents in the rebuilding process fosters a sense of control and purpose amid instability. Even small-scale actions—like creating temporary green spaces—carry profound meaning. Activities such as community gardening or public art workshops offer stability and help restore normalcy. Spaces for expression—like murals or storytelling events—help residents to process trauma and reconnect with others. Initiatives such as community seed banks, aimed at restoring war-torn ecosystems by propagating phytoremediation seeds and raising awareness of the conflict’s environmental impact, can also foster a sense of purpose and agency. These “quick and dirty” interventions build collaboration, solidarity, and belonging, evolving into lasting spaces that preserve community resilience.

The design begins with material exploration, inspired by initiatives like Zero Waste Kharkiv that reframe war debris as a valuable resource. Cataloging available materials and using photo collages to study spatial and formal relationships embeds material thinking into the design process. A clear circulation framework then organizes the site, linking public, semi-private, and private spaces. A north-south pedestrian axis connects the metro station to Barabashovo Market, while an east-west route links to the Kharkiv River—embedding the project into broader urban and ecological systems. Flexible spaces support a range of uses, from aid distribution to public celebrations. Features like a community lawn that doubles as a helicopter landing zone and a multipurpose center ensure long-term preparedness. A local seed bank, integrated into the community garden, supports both ecological restoration and food security.

The vacant land around Akademika Pavlova Station—serving as both shelter and transit hub—can be reimagined as a flexible public space that addresses immediate needs while laying the groundwork for long-term recovery. It transforms war-induced devastation into an opportunity for more resilient community. At the regional scale, its position along a potential commercial spine and near the Kharkiv River allows it to link economic and ecological systems. Quick-win projects like this can catalyze broader development, delivering visible impact, creating jobs, and rebuilding trust over time.

title: From Separation to Ambiguity
location: Harmony Circle, New Orleans, Louisiana, United States
summary: A proposal for Harmony Circle in New Orleans that brings layered cultural memories into dialogue through monument fragments, tactile materials, and shifting gradients of wetness.
story: New Orleans and the Mississippi River exist in a state of perpetual liminality—neither fully land nor water, neither defined by a single culture or race. But over time, levees rose, drawing harder lines between water and land. Social and environmental divides converged, pushing many underserved communities into the city’s most flood-prone areas. What was once fluid—ecologically and socially—began to harden into separation. The site, located at the threshold between racially diverse neighborhoods, was once envisioned as a civic common. Over time, it became a stage for political symbolism, reinforcing a singular and exclusionary narrative.

This project proposes a shift—from separation to ambiguity. Socially, it does not seek resolution through a single narrative of unity but instead holds space for tension to be seen and shared. The design creates a platform for multiple stories to coexist, using materials with distinct cultural references to reflect the layered identities of New Orleans. Fragments of the removed monument are redistributed—not as objects of reverence, but as participatory surfaces for community expression, as reflections of evolving social temperament. As James Baldwin reminds us, “Not everything that is faced can be changed. But nothing can be changed until it is faced.” Our proposal invites multiplicity, dialogue and confrontation.

Environmentally, the project treats land and water not as opposites, but as varying degrees of wetness. Subtle topographic modulation allows the site to hold water during rain and release it during dry periods. Materials are chosen for their capacity to absorb, retain, or repel moisture, creating gradients of wet and dry that shift with the weather. Rather than a hard edge, the threshold between land and water is felt bodily—through pooled water, filtered mist, and softened ground. Visitors encounter the site through the skin, through atmospheric change. Amid heat, water connects across age, race, and background with moments of shared bodily relief.

By revealing tension rather than erasing it, the site becomes a space where information is exchanged, contradictions emerge, and meanings are continually deposited. Here, ambiguity becomes the medium through which memory, climate, and culture coalesce—unfinished, alive, and open to encounter.

title: Whispers Beyond the Looking Glass
summary: An invitation to listen to plants: artificial topiaries, distorted perspectives, and a singing tree lead visitors through a looking glass into a secret garden, questioning how we perceive living nature.
story: Once upon a time, there was a singing tree deep in the forest…

From afar, it appears to be an ordinary garden — lush and well-tended. Yet the illusion fractures the moment your fingers graze the surface of the disproportionate topiaries at the entrance — the odd rubbery texture and the unchanging greenness unsettle your expectations. Mismatched scales, peculiar textures, and warped spatial perspectives confuse your sense of space. In this disoriented garden, sporadic hums from trees become the only guide, beckoning you deeper into the Secret Garden beyond the portals of the Looking Glass.

This garden is a quest for vegetal agency. Often viewed as passive or mere resources, plants are frequently undervalued for their intrinsic complexity. By playfully amplifying the contrast between the “artificial and living” and “static and unpredictable”, the garden invites visitors to reconsider their tendency to oversimplify nature to fit within human cognitive limits and aesthetic preference. The personified singing tree becomes a portal — an invitation to transcend anthropocentric perceptions and recognize plants as expressive beings in the world.
Sunlight no longer simply appears; it leaves a taste on the air. As the leaves dance in the wind, can you hear all the voices of the plants now?

title: Stitching Kingston, Community to Coast
location: Barnes Gully and Parade Gardens, Kingston, Jamaica
summary: Stitching Kingston connects communities to the harbourfront through a network of gullies, combining community-led waste management, public spaces, and decentralized water filtration along Barnes Gully.
story: Jamaica has long grappled with challenges in developing its harbourfront, primarily hindered by solid waste pollution and territorial mindset from surrounding communities. Our research indicates that for successful redevelopment, solutions must extend beyond the immediate harbourfront area to address these broader issues. Central to these challenges is the stormwater drainage system—gullies that cut through the city and channel waste directly to the harbourfront. Notably, approximately 50% of the communities along these gullies are informal settlements, which have become hotspots for illicit activities including illegal dumping, raw sewage discharge, and gang violence. These conditions reflect deeper systemic problems in these communities, such as inadequate waste management services, entrenched territorial mindsets, and limited economic opportunities.

Our vision aims to bridge community divisions by recognizing and enhancing existing community assets along sub-community boundaries and along the gullies, integrating essential public services. We propose using Barnes Gully as a pilot project. Strategically positioned through downtown Kingston and serving as a crucial access point from the airport and cruise ship terminals. We zoom into a part of the Barnes Gully intersecting with the Parade Gardens community, chosen for its critical location as a gateway community and its proximity to the harbourfront.

We plan to bridge internal community divisions by introducing a decentralized waste collection system and enhancing community assets along boundaries by proposing community-driven programs. Life Yard, an influential local organization, has demonstrated success in uniting the community by recycling waste, and urban farming, serving as a model for our community-led waste management efforts. Building on this, we plan to set up a community-led solid waste management organization. This will involve electing environmental representatives to manage waste collection, education, and maintenance, trained, and supported by the NSWMA and partners. Green incentives will enable residents to exchange recyclables for planting seeds, with the help of the National Tree Planting Initiative will enhance community green infrastructure. Furthermore, we intend to utilize vacant spaces around these community assets to create pocket spaces for waste management centers and community gardens, fostering interaction and knowledge exchange. Secondly, our strategy also includes transforming the areas around Barnes Gully into a shared community resource. We will identify community assets along the gully and enhance them through proposed programs. We plan to develop commercial plazas at key points along the gully and introduce compost sites and gardens around educational facilities to amplify their impact. Additionally, addressing sewage pollution, we propose implementing a series of decentralized filtration strategies starting within the community and extending to a filtration buffer along the gully edges, to treat sewage before it reaches the gully. We also advocate for periodic cleanup initiatives led by local communities at the end of each gully.

Our comprehensive approach transforms the perception of gullies from negative to positive, potentially creating an integrated green network across the city. This initiative will not only address the environmental and social challenges but also lay the groundwork for the successful redevelopment of Jamaica’s harbourfront.

title: Back to Roots
summary: A landscape proposal told through a graphic novel, imagining cultural continuity and renewed relations with land around Lake Okeechobee.
story: Back to Roots is a speculative landscape design project presented as a graphic novel. Historical research grounds the story, while fictional characters and proposed interventions explore how a landscape marked by displacement might be transformed into a place that sustains memory and cultural continuity.

The comic follows Osceola, a fictional Seminole elder, as he revisits memories of his grandmother and childhood. His story connects the loss of home and language with changing relationships to land and water. In conversation with landscape architect Allison, these memories become the starting point for a proposed preserve, where planting, gathering, and the changing forest allow people to encounter different layers of history.

Within the existing forest, the preserve brings together a memorial garden, an experimental planting field, and a medicine wheel garden. Annual digging and flooding would expose the ground and cause trees to die, giving material form to displacement. Fallen trees would then become compost for cultivated plants. This uneasy cycle places an expression of loss alongside the possibility of renewal, connecting remembrance with the ongoing practice and transmission of plant knowledge.

Through collage, dialogue, maps, and successive landscape scenes, the book makes time part of the design. Its final chapter extends the imagined initiative into landscapes shaped by sugarcane cultivation, while leaving its economic consequences unresolved. Back to Roots asks how cultural continuity might be sustained within a changing landscape, and what responsibilities arise when remembrance becomes a continuing practice of care.
